title: Pontianak Kadriyah Sultanate
capsule: The Kadriyah Sultanate of Pontianak (Kesultanan Pontianak) was founded on 23 October 1771 at the confluence of the Kapuas and Landak rivers in western Borneo by Syarif Abdurrahman al-Kadrie, a Hadhrami Arab sayyid who had established himself as a regional power by marrying into the Bugis elite. A Dutch treaty of 1779 formalised a cooperative relationship with the VOC; the sultanate traded gold, diamonds, and sago while the Dutch used it as a counterweight to the Lanfang Republic's Chinese mining communities. Dutch suzerainty tightened through the nineteenth century, and in 1944 the Japanese occupation regime executed Sultan Syarif Muhammad and approximately 1,500 members of the Pontianak elite in the Mandor Affair. The territory was integrated into independent Indonesia in 1950.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The sultanate's urban core and 1779 treaty boundaries are documented in Dutch colonial records; control over the Borneo interior was fluctuating and never formally delimited.
